**Your resolution didn't fail. You stopped counting.**

Every January the same post goes around: most resolutions are dead by February. Everyone nods. Nobody asks why that's supposed to be bad news.

It isn't. Most attempts at anything hard fail. That's what "hard" means. The problem isn't the failure rate. It's that people score one attempt, call the result final, and wait eleven months to try again with the same plan.

I quit smoking on the fourth serious attempt. I've been smoke-free six years. By the usual scoring, I failed three times. By any useful scoring, I ran three experiments.

Attempt two lasted five weeks and broke at a wedding. At the time that felt like a verdict. It was actually the most useful thing that happened all year, because it told me exactly where my plan had a hole: drinking, in a crowd, with people I don't see often. I'd never have found that by thinking harder. I found it by breaking.

The first three attempts, between them, gave me my trigger list. First coffee of the day. Driving. My brother. Attempt four wasn't more willpower. It was the same person with a map of where the previous three went off the road, and a plan for each spot. It held.

So here's the only resolution advice I'll offer.

Stop measuring whether the resolution survived. Measure how many attempts you made and what each one told you. An attempt that breaks in week five and leaves you with a written note saying *where* and *why* is worth more than one that limps along to March on vague good intentions and fades without a lesson.

Concretely: when it breaks, and it will, write down the date, the place, who you were with, what you'd been doing in the hour before. Don't editorialise. Don't write "I was weak." Write "Saturday, wedding, third drink, outside with the smokers." That's a finding. Then plan the next attempt around that finding specifically, and start it as soon as you've written the note. Not next January. Now.

One attempt per year is a terrible experimental design. Four attempts in eighteen months, each one patching the hole the last one found, is how things actually get quit.

You're not failing. You're running trials. Just make sure you keep the results.

**Stop Whining About Your Failed Resolution**

The statistics are everywhere: by the second week of February, 80% of New Year’s resolutions are dead in the water. Naturally, the internet is flooded with soft-focus articles telling you to "give yourself grace" and "be kind to yourself."

We’re not doing that today.

The problem isn’t that your resolution failed. The problem is your framing. "Most resolutions fail" is the entirely wrong way to look at behavioral change. What you need to understand is that most *attempts* fail.

Look at the clinical data on habit cessation. Depending on the study, the average person takes between six and thirty serious attempts to finally quit smoking for good. If you succeed on attempt number one, you aren’t morally superior; you’re just a statistical anomaly. The rest of us actually need the failures.

Some of you know I smoked for 15 years. I finally quit six years ago, but it took me four serious, grinding attempts to get there.

Attempt number two was looking great. I made it five solid weeks. Then I went to a wedding, had a few drinks, and the whole thing fell apart before the cake was cut. That wasn’t a failure of character. It was a failure of intelligence. I didn't realize that weddings combined with alcohol were my biggest structural vulnerability.

The earlier attempts taught me the rest of the list. I learned that my first morning coffee, my daily commute, and hanging out with my brother were all localized landmines. By the time I geared up for attempt number four, I wasn't relying on blind willpower. I had a tactical plan specifically designed to neutralize the wedding, the coffee, the car, and my brother.

Stop buying into the self-help industry’s jargon. This isn't about "systems versus goals" or manifesting a new you. It is about cold, hard data collection. Every time your resolution falls apart, you are gathering critical information about exactly what breaks you. Each collapse exposes a trigger you didn't plan for.

Stop evaluating yourself based on a binary outcome of success or failure. Start counting your attempts. If your New Year’s resolution just went up in smoke, do an autopsy on it. Figure out the exact moment, person, or stressor that cracked you.

You didn't fail. You just collected the necessary data for your next attempt. Now use it.

**Why your resolution is already dying, and it isn't your fault**

Every January I used to think the problem was me. I'd pick something, go hard for three weeks, then quietly stop, and I'd file it under "lost motivation," as if motivation were petrol and I'd simply run out.

I don't think that anymore, because of Welsh.

About two years ago I started learning Welsh on an app. I am not Welsh. I have no plan to move to Wales. By any sensible measure this is the least necessary thing I do. And yet I'm on a 700-day streak, which is longer than I have kept up anything that wasn't a job or a mortgage.

The difference isn't that I wanted it more. I've wanted plenty of things more. The difference is that my daughter, who is twelve, does the same app, and at dinner we compare streaks. That's it. That's the whole system. Nobody is keeping score, except that we both obviously are.

Every other resolution I've made had something in common: nobody would have noticed if I stopped. I could have skipped the running and the world would have shrugged. I could have let the reading list rot and no one at dinner would have said, "So how's that going?" The resolution lived entirely inside my head, and my head is a terrible landlord. It evicts tenants the moment they get boring.

What we call losing motivation, I think, is mostly this: the goal was private, and private things have no cost of quitting. There's no awkward moment. There's no "oh, you stopped?" You just... don't do it one day, and then the next, and the resolution dissolves so gently you can't even say when it died.

Welsh didn't survive because I'm disciplined. It survived because a twelve-year-old would have asked, with the faint cruelty only twelve-year-olds can manage, why my number had gone back to zero. Three hundred days in, the lessons were genuinely dull. The dinner conversation wasn't.

So here's the reframe I'd offer instead of the usual advice about starting small and writing things down. Stop asking whether you want this enough. Ask who is going to notice if you stop. If the honest answer is "nobody," you don't have a resolution. You have a thought.

Find a witness. Preferably one who'll be a bit smug about it.

Every January, millions of us participate in a beautiful, collective delusion: the New Year’s resolution. We are suddenly convinced that as the clock strikes midnight, some magical atmospheric shift will instantly transform us from perfectly adequate humans into highly disciplined, green-juice-drinking, marathon-running machines.

I am, of course, absolutely guilty of this. If you look closely at my bank statements from a few years ago, you will find a painfully optimistic charge on January 2nd for a premium gym membership. I went all in. I bought the expensive moisture-wicking shirts. I bought one of those giant water bottles that aggressively yells at you to hydrate. For three glorious weeks, I was unstoppable. But by the second week of February, my pristine gym shoes had retired to the darkest corner of my closet, and the only heavy lifting I was doing was carrying Thai takeout from the front porch.

Why do we do this to ourselves? Why do most resolutions crash and burn before Valentine’s Day?

The main culprit is that we try to change our entire personality overnight. We don’t just want to read more; we want to read a book a week while simultaneously learning conversational French and giving up sugar cold turkey. We treat our lives like an extreme home makeover show, relying entirely on a sudden burst of willpower. But motivation is a notoriously fickle friend. It is loud and exciting on New Year's Eve, but it completely ghosts you on a freezing Tuesday morning when your alarm goes off at 5:30 AM.

This year, instead of setting ourselves up for a spectacular February burnout, I am trying something different: micro-habits.

The idea behind micro-habits is to make your goal so ridiculously small that you cannot possibly fail. Instead of resolving to work out for an hour every day, commit to doing exactly two push-ups before your morning shower. Instead of vowing to read fifty books this year, aim to read one single page before you go to sleep.

It sounds almost suspiciously easy, but that is the entire point. By setting the bar on the floor, you bypass your brain’s natural resistance to massive change. Two push-ups often turn into ten, and one page naturally turns into a chapter. And even if they don't, you still kept your promise to yourself.

So, as we stare down another January, let’s give ourselves a break. Let's aim a little lower, celebrate the tiny victories, and save our money on the moisture-wicking shirts.

## Outline (5 minutes, ~650 words spoken)

**0:00 — Open on the August migration** *(opening paragraph below)*
One story, told plainly. Constraint dropped, three weeks to trace, author couldn't explain the change. Land on the line: nobody did anything wrong by the rules we had. That's the problem.

**0:50 — Say what this talk is not**
"I'm not here to tell you AI coding tools are good or bad. They're staying. New hires ramp in about half the time they used to. Pull requests are up sixty percent since spring. The question isn't whether we use them. It's who is responsible for what they produce."

**1:20 — Where the cost actually landed**
The number for the whole room: two senior engineers went from about four hours a week reviewing code to about eleven. That's nearly a day each, every week, reading code someone else generated and didn't fully read themselves. Translate it for sales/ops/compliance: *imagine your contract volume went up sixty percent, and every contract now needs legal to read it twice because the person who sent it can't tell you what's in clause 9.* The work didn't disappear. It moved — to the most expensive people in the room.

**2:20 — The rule, in three parts**
State it as a policy they could repeat back:
1. **The author owns every line.** If you merge it, you can explain it. Not "the tool suggested it" — what it does and why.
2. **"The AI wrote it" is never an answer in a postmortem.** Same as "the intern wrote it" never was. You reviewed it, you shipped it, it's yours.
3. **PRs over 400 changed lines get split.** Not because small is virtuous, but because nobody — not the author, not the reviewer — can actually hold 400 lines in their head. The August migration would have been caught in a PR you could read in one sitting.

**3:30 — Why this is good for the engineers, not just the reviewers**
Pre-empt the objection. This isn't a speed limit. If you're using the tool well, you already own your lines and this rule costs you nothing. It only bites when someone's shipping code they haven't read — and that person is going to get bitten eventually anyway, in a postmortem, at 2am. Better to make it the rule now than discover it the hard way again.

**4:10 — Why the rest of the room should care**
For compliance and ops: this is the same principle as any controlled process. Output is fine. Unaccountable output isn't. For sales: three weeks of reconciliation mismatch is three weeks of customers seeing wrong numbers.

**4:40 — Close**
"Use the tool for everything you want. Just don't ask it to be responsible for you. That part's still your job." Ask for the rule to go into the engineering handbook; invite objections after.

- If yes/yes/no → delegate freely. If any flip → slow down.
- Team-level: AI-generated ≠ lower review bar. Author owns every line.

**The February Fade: Why Our New Year’s Resolutions Keep Failing**

Every December 31st, as the countdown begins, we make a silent pact with ourselves. *This* is the year. We are going to run marathons, read a book every week, quit sugar entirely, and finally organize the garage. We feel a massive surge of optimism. Yet, by the second week of February, the gyms are predictably empty, the new books are gathering dust on the nightstand, and we are right back to our old routines.

Why does this happen to us every single year? The truth is, it isn't a lack of willpower or a personal failing. It is because the traditional way we set New Year’s resolutions is fundamentally broken.

**We rely on motivation instead of systems.**
Motivation is a fleeting, unreliable emotion. It is incredibly high on January 1st when you are fueled by the collective excitement of a fresh calendar year, but it inevitably crashes when your alarm goes off at 5:30 AM on a freezing, dark Tuesday morning. Resolutions rely almost entirely on this fading feeling. Real change relies on systems. Instead of trying to white-knuckle your way to discipline, successful habit-building requires designing an environment that makes good choices effortless. Hoping you will feel like running is just a wish; putting your running shoes directly in front of the bedroom door is a system.

**We try to change our entire identity overnight.**
Most resolutions are paralyzingly vague and unrealistically massive. Declarations like "I am going to get healthy" or "I will stop wasting money" sound great at a party, but they do not give your brain a concrete, daily action to take. When we set these sweeping, monumental goals, we are essentially demanding that we wake up as a completely different human being. The human brain resists sudden, massive overhauls. It thrives on tiny, incremental steps—taking a ten-minute walk after lunch rather than committing to a daily hour of strenuous weightlifting.

**We fall into the all-or-nothing trap.**
Resolutions usually carry a strict pass/fail grade. If your goal is to eat perfectly clean, having one slice of pizza feels like a catastrophic failure. Once that pristine streak is broken, the brain whispers, *“Well, I messed up today, might as well give up completely.”* This deep-seated perfectionism is the enemy of actual progress. Growth is never a straight, upward line; it is a messy, zigzagging process of trying, failing, and course-correcting.

This year, instead of writing a massive, intimidating list of resolutions, try lowering the bar. Pick one tiny, almost laughably small habit. Focus on consistency over intensity, and give yourself the grace to be imperfect. You don't need a new calendar year to build a new life—you just need a better approach.

**Why your resolution dies in February (it's not you, it's the template)**

Every piece of advice about keeping a resolution says the same thing. Pick a time. Same time every day. Build a morning routine. Protect it.

I believed that for three years. Three Januaries in a row I set a 6am gym habit, and three Februaries in a row it died, because that's when my rotation flipped to nights. "Same time every day" is a lovely idea if your days are the same. Mine aren't. Neither are yours if you're a nurse, a tech, a porter, anyone whose week is written by a rostering system rather than a Google Calendar.

Here's what I eventually worked out. My goal wasn't badly designed. I wasn't lazy or unmotivated or any of the other things the February articles suggest. The advice was written by and for people who get up, go to work, come home, and sleep, in that order, at roughly the same hours, forever. Once you see that, every "morning routine" post reads like instructions for a kitchen you don't own. When does a morning routine happen if your morning is 7pm?

So I stopped tying the habit to a clock and tied it to an event instead. The new rule: gym is the first thing after any shift ends. Day shift, night shift, long day, doesn't matter. Badge out, go. I've kept that one for fourteen months, which is roughly thirteen months longer than the previous three attempts combined.

Why does it work? Because the shift ending is the one fixed point in a week that has none. The clock moves. Handover doesn't. You already have a thing you do without thinking the moment you finish, whether that's coffee or sitting in the car staring at nothing for ten minutes. You're not building a habit from scratch; you're bolting it onto something that already fires.

It doesn't have to be the gym. Pick whatever you wanted to do this year and ask: what's the event, not the hour? After handover. Before I eat on break. The moment I take my shoes off at home. If the answer is still "at 6am," you'll be back here next February, and I'll be glad of the company, but I'd rather you weren't.

One suggestion, then. Anchor to an event, not a clock. The clock was never yours anyway.

In reality, I was trying to force a static habit onto a chaotic schedule.

What finally worked wasn't a new planner or a motivational podcast. It was abandoning the clock entirely.

If your life does not run on a neat corporate schedule, you need event-anchored habits. Stop trying to attach your new goal to a specific hour. Drink a glass of water the second you walk through your front door. Do a five-minute stretch the moment you clock out.

Your past resolutions didn't die because you are broken. They died because the blueprint was wrong for your life. This year, pick just one thing you want to change, find a reliable event in your day, and attach it. See what happens when the habit actually fits the life you are living.

# Why Most New Year's Resolutions Fail (And It's Not Because You're Lazy)

Every January, gyms fill up, journals get their first entries, and millions of people swear this is the year everything changes. By February, most of those plans have quietly dissolved. Research consistently suggests that the vast majority of resolutions are abandoned within a few weeks. So what's going wrong?

## We mistake a wish for a plan

"Get healthier." "Save more money." "Read more." These are destinations, not directions. A resolution without a specific first step is just a hope with a deadline. When the moment comes to actually do something, there's nothing concrete to do, so we do nothing. "Walk for 20 minutes after lunch on weekdays" survives contact with real life. "Get fit" doesn't.

## We rely on motivation, which is a terrible employee

January 1st motivation is real, but it's borrowed from the novelty of a fresh start. It shows up late, leaves early, and never comes in when it's raining. People who stick with new habits don't have more willpower; they've built systems that don't require much of it. The running shoes are by the door. The savings transfer is automatic. The decision has already been made so it doesn't have to be re-made every day.

## We start at full intensity

Going from zero to six workouts a week feels committed. It's actually fragile. Big changes demand big energy, and the first week you're exhausted or sick or busy, the whole structure collapses. Then comes the real killer: the all-or-nothing mindset. Miss one day and the resolution feels "broken," so why bother continuing? Small, almost embarrassingly easy habits survive bad weeks. Ambitious ones rarely do.

## We change the behavior but not the identity

If you still see yourself as "someone who's bad with money," every budget feels like a costume you'll eventually take off. Lasting change tends to happen when the new behavior becomes part of how you see yourself. Not "I'm trying to run," but "I'm a runner, even a slow one."

## We pick a date instead of a reason

January 1st is arbitrary. There's nothing magical about it, which is exactly the problem. A resolution chosen because of the calendar often lacks the personal, specific "why" that carries people through the hard middle stretch.

## So what actually works?

Start smaller than feels reasonable. Attach the new habit to something you already do. Expect to miss days, and decide in advance that missing one never means quitting. And don't wait for January. Any Tuesday will do.

## The problem with January 1

Every New Year's resolution starts on a date nobody chose.

That sounds like a small thing. It isn't. Think about how real changes begin. Someone quits smoking the week their kid is born. Someone starts running because a doctor said a sentence they couldn't unhear. Someone finally learns to cook because the new flat is too far from any takeaway. In each case the change has a reason, and the reason has a date, and the date is whenever the reason showed up. The change is a response to something.

A resolution reverses this. The date arrives first, on its own, and then you go looking for a change to attach to it. January 1 doesn't know anything about you. It's the same day for everyone, which is exactly why it's useless as a trigger: it can't be about your life in particular, because it's about the Earth completing a lap.

So you pick something. Usually something you've vaguely wanted for a while, which is a polite way of saying something you've had plenty of chances to start and haven't. Nothing about your situation has changed since December 29. The only new thing is the number on the calendar, and the number can't carry any weight once the first week is over. It's not that you lack willpower. It's that you've asked a date to do the job a reason should be doing, and the date clocked off at midnight.

There's a real effect here, to be fair. Psychologists have found that people do feel more motivated right after a landmark like a new year or a birthday. The slate feels clean. But a feeling of freshness is not a reason, and it fades at about the speed you'd expect. The gyms know this. They sell January memberships on the assumption that you'll stop coming, and they're right often enough to build a business on it.

Meanwhile the changes that stick tend to start on a random Tuesday in March, because that's when the thing happened. Nobody writes those down. Nobody announces them. They just start, because something made them necessary, and necessity doesn't check the calendar.

So the question worth asking about a resolution isn't whether it's specific enough or small enough. It's simpler than that: if January 1 didn't exist, would you be doing this anyway? If yes, you don't need the date. If no, the date won't help.

# Why Most New Year's Resolutions Fail (And What Actually Works)

Every January, gyms fill up, journals get cracked open, and millions of us declare that *this* is the year everything changes. By February, most of those promises are quietly abandoned. Studies suggest the majority of resolutions don't survive past the first few weeks. So what goes wrong?

## We confuse motivation with momentum

New Year's Eve is a rush. The clock strikes midnight, the year feels like a blank page, and anything seems possible. But motivation is a feeling, and feelings fade. By the second week of January, the sparkle is gone and you're left with the actual, unglamorous work of changing your life. If your plan depended on feeling inspired, it was always going to collapse the moment you didn't.

## We aim too big, too fast

"Run a marathon." "Read 50 books." "Completely overhaul my diet." These are admirable goals, but they ask for a total transformation from someone who hasn't yet built the habit of running a mile or reading a chapter. When the gap between where you are and where you want to be is enormous, every day feels like failure. And nobody keeps doing something that makes them feel like a failure.

## We set outcomes, not systems

A resolution like "lose 20 pounds" tells you where you want to end up but says nothing about how to get there. Without a concrete, repeatable action, you're left relying on willpower every single day. Willpower is a terrible long-term strategy. **Why your resolution dies in February (it's not you, it's the template)**

Every piece of advice about keeping a resolution says the same thing. Pick a time. Same time every day. Build a morning routine. Protect it.

I believed that for three years. Three Januaries in a row I set a 6am gym habit, and three Februaries in a row it died, because that's when my rotation flipped to nights. "Same time every day" is a lovely idea if your days are the same. Mine aren't. Neither are yours if you're a nurse, a tech, a porter, anyone whose week is written by a rostering system rather than a Google Calendar.

Here's what I eventually worked out. My goal wasn't badly designed. I wasn't lazy or unmotivated or any of the other things the February articles suggest. The advice was written by and for people who get up, go to work, come home, and sleep, in that order, at roughly the same hours, forever. Once you see that, every "morning routine" post reads like instructions for a kitchen you don't own. When does a morning routine happen if your morning is 7pm?

So I stopped tying the habit to a clock and tied it to an event instead. The new rule: gym is the first thing after any shift ends. Day shift, night shift, long day, doesn't matter. Badge out, go. I've kept that one for fourteen months, which is roughly thirteen months longer than the previous three attempts combined.

Why does it work? Because the shift ending is the one fixed point in a week that has none. The clock moves. Handover doesn't. You already have a thing you do without thinking the moment you finish, whether that's coffee or sitting in the car staring at nothing for ten minutes. If the answer is still "at 6am," you'll be back here next February, and I'll be glad of the company, but I'd rather you weren't.

One suggestion, then. Anchor to an event, not a clock. The clock was never yours anyway.

**Your resolution didn't fail. You stopped counting.**

Every January the same post goes around: most resolutions are dead by February. Everyone nods. Nobody asks why that's supposed to be bad news.

It isn't. Most attempts at anything hard fail. That's what "hard" means. The problem isn't the failure rate. It's that people score one attempt, call the result final, and wait eleven months to try again with the same plan.

I quit smoking on the fourth serious attempt. I've been smoke-free six years. By the usual scoring, I failed three times. By any useful scoring, I ran three experiments.

Attempt two lasted five weeks and broke at a wedding. At the time that felt like a verdict. It was actually the most useful thing that happened all year, because it told me exactly where my plan had a hole: drinking, in a crowd, with people I don't see often. The first three attempts, between them, gave me my trigger list. First coffee of the day. Driving. My brother. Attempt four wasn't more willpower. It was the same person with a map of where the previous three went off the road, and a plan for each spot. It held.

Stop measuring whether the resolution survived. Measure how many attempts you made and what each one told you. You're not failing. You're running trials. Just make sure you keep the results.

## 5-Minute Talk Outline

**1. The Reality Check (1 Minute)**

* **The Thesis:** AI is a tireless, eager junior developer. It is exceptionally fast, knows every language, but lacks the crucial context of our specific systems, business logic, and user needs.
* **The Mindset Shift:** We are moving from "authors" of every line of code to "reviewers and directors" of code.

**2. The Sweet Spots: Where You *Should* Use It (1.5 Minutes)**

* **Boilerplate & Setup:** Let the AI write the scaffolding, the repetitive CRUD operations, and the standard configuration files.
* **Test Generation:** Generating standard unit tests and edge cases (though engineers must verify the assertions).
* **Rubber Duck Debugging & Explanations:** Dropping an undocumented block of legacy code into the prompt and asking, "What is this doing?"
* **The Takeaway:** Use AI for the highly predictable, low-risk "brawn" of software development.

**3. The Danger Zones: Where You *Must* Take the Wheel (1.5 Minutes)**

* **Security & Data Privacy:** AI doesn't know our threat model. It will happily suggest insecure cryptographic hashes or expose sensitive data loops if not caught.
* **Architectural Decisions:** AI solves for the immediate prompt, not for the system's long-term scalability or maintainability.
* **The "Hallucination" Tax:** Creating phantom libraries or methods that look perfectly logical but don't actually exist.
* **The Takeaway:** Never blindly commit code you don't understand well enough to explain to a peer. You own the code, not the assistant.

**4. Our Philosophy Moving Forward (1 Minute)**

* **The Golden Rule:** The engineer whose name is on the pull request is 100% responsible for the code, regardless of who (or what) typed it.
* **Call to Action:** Encourage the team to experiment with these tools to boost their velocity, share the best prompts they discover in Slack, and aggressively call out AI-generated bad practices in code reviews.
* **Closing Thought:** AI won't replace engineers, but engineers who effectively use AI will replace those who don't. Let's make sure we are the former.

# Why Most New Year's Resolutions Fail (And It's Not Because You're Lazy)

Every January, gyms fill up, journals get cracked open, and millions of people swear this is the year they finally change. By mid-February, most of those gyms are quiet again. Research consistently shows that the vast majority of resolutions are abandoned within weeks.

So what's going on? It's tempting to blame willpower, but the real reasons are more structural than moral.

## We confuse outcomes with behaviors

"Lose 20 pounds" and "write a novel" are outcomes, not actions. You can't *do* an outcome on a Tuesday morning. Resolutions that stick are built around specific, repeatable behaviors: "walk for 20 minutes after lunch" or "write 300 words before checking email." The outcome follows the behavior, not the other way around.

## January 1st is an arbitrary starting line

There's nothing about the calendar flipping that makes change easier. If anything, it's a terrible time to start. You're coming off weeks of disrupted routines, late nights, and heavy food. Starting a demanding new habit while your life is still recovering from the holidays is like beginning a marathon with a sprained ankle.

## We go too big, too fast

The excitement of a fresh start pushes people toward dramatic overhauls: new diet, new workout, new sleep schedule, all at once. This feels ambitious, but it's actually fragile. One bad week breaks everything simultaneously. Small changes feel unimpressive, but they survive contact with real life.

## We rely on motivation instead of design

Motivation is a feeling, and feelings fluctuate. The people who succeed don't necessarily want it more; they've arranged their environment so the right choice is the easy choice. Gym clothes laid out the night before. Junk food not in the house. A friend who expects you at 7am. Systems beat intentions.

Miss one workout and the whole plan feels ruined, so why bother? This is the single most common way resolutions die. A missed day is a data point, not a verdict. The real skill isn't never slipping; it's getting back on track quickly without drama.

Pick one thing. Make it small enough that you could do it on your worst day. Attach it to something you already do. Plan for failure in advance so a slip doesn't become a spiral. And don't wait for January; start the next time you have a reasonably normal week.

The goal was never a perfect streak. It was becoming someone slightly different than you were last year. That happens through accumulation, not resolution.

Every January, millions of us participate in a beautiful, collective delusion: the New Year’s resolution. We are suddenly convinced that as the clock strikes midnight, some magical atmospheric shift will instantly transform us from perfectly adequate humans into highly disciplined, green-juice-drinking, marathon-running machines.

I am, of course, absolutely guilty of this. If you look closely at my bank statements from a few years ago, you will find a painfully optimistic charge on January 2nd for a premium gym membership. I went all in. I bought the expensive moisture-wicking shirts. I bought one of those giant water bottles that aggressively yells at you to hydrate. For three glorious weeks, I was unstoppable. But by the second week of February, my pristine gym shoes had retired to the darkest corner of my closet, and the only heavy lifting I was doing was carrying Thai takeout from the front porch.

Why do we do this to ourselves? Why do most resolutions crash and burn before Valentine’s Day?

The main culprit is that we try to change our entire personality overnight. We don’t just want to read more; we want to read a book a week while simultaneously learning conversational French and giving up sugar cold turkey. We treat our lives like an extreme home makeover show, relying entirely on a sudden burst of willpower. But motivation is a notoriously fickle friend. It is loud and exciting on New Year's Eve, but it completely ghosts you on a freezing Tuesday morning when your alarm goes off at 5:30 AM.

This year, instead of setting ourselves up for a spectacular February burnout, I am trying something different: micro-habits.

The idea behind micro-habits is to make your goal so ridiculously small that you cannot possibly fail. Instead of resolving to work out for an hour every day, commit to doing exactly two push-ups before your morning shower. Instead of vowing to read fifty books this year, aim to read one single page before you go to sleep.

It sounds almost suspiciously easy, but that is the entire point. By setting the bar on the floor, you bypass your brain’s natural resistance to massive change. Two push-ups often turn into ten, and one page naturally turns into a chapter. And even if they don't, you still kept your promise to yourself.

So, as we stare down another January, let’s give ourselves a break. Let's aim a little lower, celebrate the tiny victories, and save our money on the moisture-wicking shirts.

**Why your resolution is already dying, and it isn't your fault**

Every January I used to think the problem was me. I'd pick something, go hard for three weeks, then quietly stop, and I'd file it under "lost motivation," as if motivation were petrol and I'd simply run out.

I don't think that anymore, because of Welsh.

About two years ago I started learning Welsh on an app. I am not Welsh. I have no plan to move to Wales. By any sensible measure this is the least necessary thing I do. And yet I'm on a 700-day streak, which is longer than I have kept up anything that wasn't a job or a mortgage.

The difference isn't that I wanted it more. I've wanted plenty of things more. The difference is that my daughter, who is twelve, does the same app, and at dinner we compare streaks. That's it. That's the whole system. Nobody is keeping score, except that we both obviously are.

Every other resolution I've made had something in common: nobody would have noticed if I stopped. I could have skipped the running and the world would have shrugged. I could have let the reading list rot and no one at dinner would have said, "So how's that going?" The resolution lived entirely inside my head, and my head is a terrible landlord. It evicts tenants the moment they get boring.

What we call losing motivation, I think, is mostly this: the goal was private, and private things have no cost of quitting. There's no awkward moment. There's no "oh, you stopped?" You just... don't do it one day, and then the next, and the resolution dissolves so gently you can't even say when it died.

Welsh didn't survive because I'm disciplined. It survived because a twelve-year-old would have asked, with the faint cruelty only twelve-year-olds can manage, why my number had gone back to zero. Three hundred days in, the lessons were genuinely dull. The dinner conversation wasn't.

So here's the reframe I'd offer instead of the usual advice about starting small and writing things down. Stop asking whether you want this enough. Ask who is going to notice if you stop. If the honest answer is "nobody," you don't have a resolution. You have a thought.

Find a witness. Preferably one who'll be a bit smug about it.

# Why Most New Year's Resolutions Fail (And What Actually Works)

Every January, gyms fill up, journals get cracked open, and millions of us declare that *this* is the year everything changes. By February, most of those promises are quietly abandoned. Studies suggest the majority of resolutions don't survive past the first few weeks. So what goes wrong?

## We confuse motivation with momentum

New Year's Eve is a rush. The clock strikes midnight, the year feels like a blank page, and anything seems possible. But motivation is a feeling, and feelings fade. By the second week of January, the sparkle is gone and you're left with the actual, unglamorous work of changing your life. If your plan depended on feeling inspired, it was always going to collapse the moment you didn't.

## We aim too big, too fast

"Run a marathon." "Read 50 books." "Completely overhaul my diet." These are admirable goals, but they ask for a total transformation from someone who hasn't yet built the habit of running a mile or reading a chapter. When the gap between where you are and where you want to be is enormous, every day feels like failure. And nobody keeps doing something that makes them feel like a failure.

## We set outcomes, not systems

A resolution like "lose 20 pounds" tells you where you want to end up but says nothing about how to get there. Without a concrete, repeatable action, you're left relying on willpower every single day. Willpower is a terrible long-term strategy. The people who actually change are the ones who decide *when* and *where* the behavior happens: "I walk for 20 minutes after lunch, every weekday." Boring, specific, and sustainable.

## We treat one slip as the end

Miss one workout, eat one slice of cake, skip one day of journaling, and suddenly the whole resolution feels broken. This all-or-nothing thinking is probably the single biggest killer of good intentions. Real progress is messy. The question isn't whether you'll stumble; it's whether you'll pick things back up the next day.

## So what actually works?

Start smaller than feels reasonable. Attach the new habit to something you already do. Track it somewhere visible. And when you inevitably miss a day, make the rule simple: never miss twice.

The calendar flipping over doesn't change you. Showing up, imperfectly and repeatedly, does. You don't need a new year for that. You just need tomorrow.

## The problem with January 1

Every New Year's resolution starts on a date nobody chose.

That sounds like a small thing. It isn't. Think about how real changes begin. Someone quits smoking the week their kid is born. Someone starts running because a doctor said a sentence they couldn't unhear. Someone finally learns to cook because the new flat is too far from any takeaway. In each case the change has a reason, and the reason has a date, and the date is whenever the reason showed up. The change is a response to something.

A resolution reverses this. The date arrives first, on its own, and then you go looking for a change to attach to it. January 1 doesn't know anything about you. It's the same day for everyone, which is exactly why it's useless as a trigger: it can't be about your life in particular, because it's about the Earth completing a lap.

So you pick something. Usually something you've vaguely wanted for a while, which is a polite way of saying something you've had plenty of chances to start and haven't. Nothing about your situation has changed since December 29. The only new thing is the number on the calendar, and the number can't carry any weight once the first week is over. It's not that you lack willpower. It's that you've asked a date to do the job a reason should be doing, and the date clocked off at midnight.

There's a real effect here, to be fair. Psychologists have found that people do feel more motivated right after a landmark like a new year or a birthday. The slate feels clean. But a feeling of freshness is not a reason, and it fades at about the speed you'd expect. The gyms know this. They sell January memberships on the assumption that you'll stop coming, and they're right often enough to build a business on it.

Meanwhile the changes that stick tend to start on a random Tuesday in March, because that's when the thing happened. Nobody writes those down. Nobody announces them. They just start, because something made them necessary, and necessity doesn't check the calendar.

So the question worth asking about a resolution isn't whether it's specific enough or small enough. It's simpler than that: if January 1 didn't exist, would you be doing this anyway? If yes, you don't need the date. If no, the date won't help.

If this sounds familiar, you aren’t alone. Studies consistently show that a staggering 80% of New Year’s resolutions collapse by the time Valentine’s Day rolls around. But why do we keep falling into the exact same trap year after year?

The biggest culprit is that **we rely on fleeting motivation instead of building resilient systems**. On January 1st, we are riding a wave of culturally mandated inspiration. We feel completely unstoppable. But motivation is an emotion, and emotions are notoriously unreliable. When the alarm goes off in a freezing, dark room on a typical Tuesday morning, motivation is nowhere to be found. If you don't have a frictionless system in place—like sleeping in your workout clothes or having your coffee maker pre-programmed—that emotional high isn't going to be enough to drag you out of bed.

**Why your resolution dies in February (it's not you, it's the template)**

Every piece of advice about keeping a resolution says the same thing. Pick a time. Same time every day. Build a morning routine. Protect it.

I've kept that one for fourteen months, which is roughly thirteen months longer than the previous three attempts combined.

You already have a thing you do without thinking the moment you finish, whether that's coffee or sitting in the car staring at nothing for ten minutes. One suggestion, then. Anchor to an event, not a clock. The clock was never yours anyway.

Motivation is highest on New Year's Eve and lowest on a cold Wednesday in late January. If your plan only works when you feel inspired, it will collapse the first time you don't. Lasting change comes from systems: a set time, a prepared environment, a default routine that runs even when you'd rather not.

The classic pattern: you miss one workout, feel like you've "broken" the resolution, and quietly give up. This all-or-nothing thinking turns a minor stumble into a complete collapse. The people who succeed aren't the ones who never miss. They're the ones who miss once and get back to it the next day.

Start smaller than feels reasonable. Instead of "exercise more," try "walk ten minutes after lunch." Instead of "read more," try "read one page before bed." Tiny goals are easy to keep, and keeping them builds the identity of someone who follows through.

Tie new habits to existing ones. Attach the new behavior to something you already do every day, so it rides along for free.

And finally, plan for failure in advance. Decide right now what you'll do when you miss a day. The answer should be boring: just start again tomorrow.

## The problem with January 1

Every New Year's resolution starts on a date nobody chose.

That sounds like a small thing. It isn't. Think about how real changes begin. Someone quits smoking the week their kid is born. Someone starts running because a doctor said a sentence they couldn't unhear. Someone finally learns to cook because the new flat is too far from any takeaway. In each case the change has a reason, and the reason has a date, and the date is whenever the reason showed up. The change is a response to something.

A resolution reverses this. The date arrives first, on its own, and then you go looking for a change to attach to it. January 1 doesn't know anything about you. It's the same day for everyone, which is exactly why it's useless as a trigger: it can't be about your life in particular, because it's about the Earth completing a lap.

So you pick something. Usually something you've vaguely wanted for a while, which is a polite way of saying something you've had plenty of chances to start and haven't. Nothing about your situation has changed since December 29. The only new thing is the number on the calendar, and the number can't carry any weight once the first week is over. It's not that you lack willpower. It's that you've asked a date to do the job a reason should be doing, and the date clocked off at midnight.

There's a real effect here, to be fair. Psychologists have found that people do feel more motivated right after a landmark like a new year or a birthday. The slate feels clean. But a feeling of freshness is not a reason, and it fades at about the speed you'd expect. The gyms know this. They sell January memberships on the assumption that you'll stop coming, and they're right often enough to build a business on it.

Meanwhile the changes that stick tend to start on a random Tuesday in March, because that's when the thing happened. Nobody writes those down. Nobody announces them. They just start, because something made them necessary, and necessity doesn't check the calendar.

So the question worth asking about a resolution isn't whether it's specific enough or small enough. It's simpler than that: if January 1 didn't exist, would you be doing this anyway? If yes, you don't need the date. If no, the date won't help.

If this sounds familiar, you aren’t alone. Studies consistently show that a staggering 80% of New Year’s resolutions collapse by the time Valentine’s Day rolls around. But why do we keep falling into the exact same trap year after year?

The biggest culprit is that **we rely on fleeting motivation instead of building resilient systems**. On January 1st, we are riding a wave of culturally mandated inspiration. We feel completely unstoppable. But motivation is an emotion, and emotions are notoriously unreliable. When the alarm goes off in a freezing, dark room on a typical Tuesday morning, motivation is nowhere to be found. If you don't have a frictionless system in place—like sleeping in your workout clothes or having your coffee maker pre-programmed—that emotional high isn't going to be enough to drag you out of bed.

Furthermore, **we set destinations instead of plotting a course**. A resolution like "I'm going to get healthy this year" or "I'm going to save more money" is a wish, not a plan. It lacks the critical scaffolding of the everyday execution. When goals are broad and undefined, they overwhelm us, and our brains need concrete, bite-sized directives to take action. Promising yourself, "I will walk for twenty minutes on my lunch break every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday," gives your brain a specific instruction it can execute. Just telling yourself to "get fit" only gives it anxiety.

Finally, **we fall victim to the all-or-nothing illusion**. We convince ourselves that transformation requires a flawless, unbroken streak. So, when we inevitably miss a workout, eat the donut, or skip the journaling session, we feel like we’ve failed the entire mission. The streak is broken, so we throw in the towel completely. We forget that progress isn't a fragile glass sculpture; it's a messy, resilient process. Missing one single day doesn't ruin your goal unless you let the guilt stop you from trying again tomorrow.

This year, maybe it’s time to abandon the grand, sweeping New Year’s resolution entirely. Instead of trying to reinvent yourself overnight, focus on building one microscopic, sustainable habit. You don't need a brand new you. You just need a slightly better Tuesday.

# Why Most New Year's Resolutions Fail (And What to Do Instead)

Every January, gyms fill up, journals get cracked open, and millions of people declare that *this* is the year everything changes. By February, most of those gyms are quiet again. Studies consistently suggest that the vast majority of resolutions are abandoned within a few months, and many don't survive the first few weeks.

So what's going on? It's not a lack of willpower or a character flaw. Resolutions fail for predictable reasons, and once you see them, you can work around them.

## 1. They're built on a date, not a decision

January 1st is arbitrary. The calendar flipping over doesn't change your schedule, your stress levels, or your habits. Many resolutions are made because it's "the time to make resolutions," not because the person has genuinely decided they're ready for change. A goal chosen for the occasion rarely has the roots to survive a bad week.

## 2. They're too big and too vague

"Get healthy." "Read more." "Save money." These sound great, but they're outcomes, not actions. Without a clear next step, your brain has nothing to do on a Tuesday afternoon. Vague goals also make it impossible to know if you're succeeding, which drains motivation fast.

## 3. They rely on motivation instead of systems

Motivation is highest on New Year's Eve and lowest on a cold Wednesday in late January. If your plan only works when you feel inspired, it will collapse the first time you don't. Lasting change comes from systems: a set time, a prepared environment, a default routine that runs even when you'd rather not.

## 4. They treat one slip as total failure

The classic pattern: you miss one workout, feel like you've "broken" the resolution, and quietly give up. This all-or-nothing thinking turns a minor stumble into a complete collapse. The people who succeed aren't the ones who never miss. They're the ones who miss once and get back to it the next day.

## What actually works

Start smaller than feels reasonable. Instead of "exercise more," try "walk ten minutes after lunch." Instead of "read more," try "read one page before bed." Tiny goals are easy to keep, and keeping them builds the identity of someone who follows through.

Tie new habits to existing ones. Attach the new behavior to something you already do every day, so it rides along for free.

And finally, plan for failure in advance. Decide right now what you'll do when you miss a day. The answer should be boring: just start again tomorrow.

Resolutions don't fail because people are weak. They fail because they're designed to. Design yours differently.

**Why your resolution dies in February (it's not you, it's the template)**

Every piece of advice about keeping a resolution says the same thing. Pick a time. Same time every day. Build a morning routine. Protect it.

I believed that for three years. Three Januaries in a row I set a 6am gym habit, and three Februaries in a row it died, because that's when my rotation flipped to nights. "Same time every day" is a lovely idea if your days are the same. Mine aren't. Neither are yours if you're a nurse, a tech, a porter, anyone whose week is written by a rostering system rather than a Google Calendar.

Here's what I eventually worked out. My goal wasn't badly designed. I wasn't lazy or unmotivated or any of the other things the February articles suggest. The advice was written by and for people who get up, go to work, come home, and sleep, in that order, at roughly the same hours, forever. Once you see that, every "morning routine" post reads like instructions for a kitchen you don't own. When does a morning routine happen if your morning is 7pm?

So I stopped tying the habit to a clock and tied it to an event instead. The new rule: gym is the first thing after any shift ends. Day shift, night shift, long day, doesn't matter. Badge out, go. I've kept that one for fourteen months, which is roughly thirteen months longer than the previous three attempts combined.

Why does it work? Because the shift ending is the one fixed point in a week that has none. The clock moves. Handover doesn't. You already have a thing you do without thinking the moment you finish, whether that's coffee or sitting in the car staring at nothing for ten minutes. You're not building a habit from scratch; you're bolting it onto something that already fires.

It doesn't have to be the gym. Pick whatever you wanted to do this year and ask: what's the event, not the hour? After handover. Before I eat on break. The moment I take my shoes off at home. If the answer is still "at 6am," you'll be back here next February, and I'll be glad of the company, but I'd rather you weren't.

One suggestion, then. Anchor to an event, not a clock. The clock was never yours anyway.

## 5-Minute Talk Outline: AI Coding Assistants in Practice

**I. The Reality of Our AI Adoption (1 Minute)**

* **The Baseline:** Acknowledge that the tools are officially here, licenses are active, and widespread adoption is already happening.
* **The Core Thesis:** AI is a highly capable accelerator for the mundane, but a dangerous substitute for critical engineering thought. We need a shared understanding of where it helps and where it hurts.

**II. The Green Zone: Where We Should Be Using AI (1 Minute)**

* **Boilerplate & Scaffolding:** Eliminating the friction of setting up new components, writing standard API wrappers, and generating syntax.

* **Code Comprehension:** Translating unfamiliar legacy code or quickly onboarding PMs and engineers into new repositories.

* **The "Confident but Wrong" Trap:** AI hallucinates plausibly. It will generate code that compiles beautifully, uses the right naming conventions, and entirely misses a subtle race condition or security vulnerability.

* **Zero-Trust Code Review:** Code generated by AI requires *more* scrutiny, not less. Review it as if it were written by a highly caffeinated intern who means well but doesn't know our stack.

**Why your resolution is already dying, and it isn't your fault**

Every January I used to think the problem was me. I'd pick something, go hard for three weeks, then quietly stop, and I'd file it under "lost motivation," as if motivation were petrol and I'd simply run out.

I don't think that anymore, because of Welsh.

About two years ago I started learning Welsh on an app. I am not Welsh. I have no plan to move to Wales. By any sensible measure this is the least necessary thing I do. And yet I'm on a 700-day streak, which is longer than I have kept up anything that wasn't a job or a mortgage.

The difference isn't that I wanted it more. I've wanted plenty of things more. The difference is that my daughter, who is twelve, does the same app, and at dinner we compare streaks. That's it. That's the whole system. Nobody is keeping score, except that we both obviously are.

Every other resolution I've made had something in common: nobody would have noticed if I stopped. I could have skipped the running and the world would have shrugged. I could have let the reading list rot and no one at dinner would have said, "So how's that going?" The resolution lived entirely inside my head, and my head is a terrible landlord. It evicts tenants the moment they get boring.

What we call losing motivation, I think, is mostly this: the goal was private, and private things have no cost of quitting. There's no awkward moment. There's no "oh, you stopped?" You just... don't do it one day, and then the next, and the resolution dissolves so gently you can't even say when it died.

Welsh didn't survive because I'm disciplined. It survived because a twelve-year-old would have asked, with the faint cruelty only twelve-year-olds can manage, why my number had gone back to zero. Three hundred days in, the lessons were genuinely dull. The dinner conversation wasn't.

So here's the reframe I'd offer instead of the usual advice about starting small and writing things down. Stop asking whether you want this enough. Ask who is going to notice if you stop. If the honest answer is "nobody," you don't have a resolution. You have a thought.

Find a witness. Preferably one who'll be a bit smug about it.

Every January 1st, gyms are packed to capacity, productivity planners are sold out, and kale flies off the grocery store shelves. By the second week of February? The treadmill has become a remarkably expensive clothes hanger, and we are right back to our regular routines.

Research consistently shows that roughly 80% of New Year's resolutions are abandoned before winter even ends. We tend to internalize this as a personal failure of willpower or discipline. In reality, it is almost entirely a failure of strategy.

## Vagueness is the Enemy

The most common resolutions are sweeping declarations like "I want to get in shape," "I will save more money," or "I want to read more." These are not actionable goals; they are simply wishes. When a resolution lacks specific, measurable parameters, your brain experiences decision fatigue. When the alarm goes off at 6:00 AM, **"get in shape"** requires you to figure out exactly what that means in the moment—which usually leads to hitting the snooze button.

To fix this, swap vague aspirations for concrete habits. Instead of "read more," commit to reading ten pages of a book every night in bed before turning out the light.

## The All-or-Nothing Trap

You stick to a perfectly balanced diet for twelve days straight. On day thirteen, someone brings fresh donuts into the breakroom, and you eat one. The typical psychological response is to assume the entire endeavor is ruined, order a large pizza for dinner, and tell yourself you will try again next year. This perfectionist mindset treats a minor, inevitable slip-up as a total systemic failure.

Expect the friction. A highly effective strategy to combat this is adopting a **"never miss twice"** rule. If you skip one workout or overspend your budget one day, you haven't failed—your only objective for the following day is simply getting back to your baseline.

## Relying on a Fairweather Friend

January energy is a unique, fleeting high fueled by the calendar change. Relying on that initial surge of motivation to carry you through a dark, rainy Tuesday in March is a losing bet. Motivation dictates how you feel in a given moment, but **systems dictate what you actually do**.

Stop trying to manufacture motivation and start reducing friction. If you want to run in the mornings, put your shoes next to the door and sleep in your athletic clothes. Design your environment so that the right choice is the path of least resistance.

True change does not care about the date on the calendar. It relies on sustainable, boring, everyday consistency. You don't need a new year to completely reinvent your life—you just need a slightly better system for tomorrow morning.

**Stop Whining About Your Failed Resolution**

The statistics are everywhere: by the second week of February, 80% of New Year’s resolutions are dead in the water. Naturally, the internet is flooded with soft-focus articles telling you to "give yourself grace" and "be kind to yourself."

We’re not doing that today.

The problem isn’t that your resolution failed. The problem is your framing. "Most resolutions fail" is the entirely wrong way to look at behavioral change. What you need to understand is that most *attempts* fail.

Look at the clinical data on habit cessation. Depending on the study, the average person takes between six and thirty serious attempts to finally quit smoking for good. If you succeed on attempt number one, you aren’t morally superior; you’re just a statistical anomaly. The rest of us actually need the failures.

Some of you know I smoked for 15 years. I finally quit six years ago, but it took me four serious, grinding attempts to get there.

Attempt number two was looking great. I made it five solid weeks. Then I went to a wedding, had a few drinks, and the whole thing fell apart before the cake was cut. That wasn’t a failure of character. It was a failure of intelligence. I didn't realize that weddings combined with alcohol were my biggest structural vulnerability.

The earlier attempts taught me the rest of the list. I learned that my first morning coffee, my daily commute, and hanging out with my brother were all localized landmines. By the time I geared up for attempt number four, I wasn't relying on blind willpower. I had a tactical plan specifically designed to neutralize the wedding, the coffee, the car, and my brother.

Stop buying into the self-help industry’s jargon. This isn't about "systems versus goals" or manifesting a new you. It is about cold, hard data collection. Every time your resolution falls apart, you are gathering critical information about exactly what breaks you. Each collapse exposes a trigger you didn't plan for.

Stop evaluating yourself based on a binary outcome of success or failure. Start counting your attempts. If your New Year’s resolution just went up in smoke, do an autopsy on it. Figure out the exact moment, person, or stressor that cracked you.

You didn't fail. You just collected the necessary data for your next attempt. Now use it.

**Your resolution didn't fail. You stopped counting.**

Every January the same post goes around: most resolutions are dead by February. Everyone nods. Nobody asks why that's supposed to be bad news.

It isn't. Most attempts at anything hard fail. That's what "hard" means. The problem isn't the failure rate. It's that people score one attempt, call the result final, and wait eleven months to try again with the same plan.

I quit smoking on the fourth serious attempt. I've been smoke-free six years. By the usual scoring, I failed three times. By any useful scoring, I ran three experiments.

Attempt two lasted five weeks and broke at a wedding. At the time that felt like a verdict. It was actually the most useful thing that happened all year, because it told me exactly where my plan had a hole: drinking, in a crowd, with people I don't see often. I'd never have found that by thinking harder. I found it by breaking.

The first three attempts, between them, gave me my trigger list. First coffee of the day. Driving. My brother. Attempt four wasn't more willpower. It was the same person with a map of where the previous three went off the road, and a plan for each spot. It held.

So here's the only resolution advice I'll offer.

Stop measuring whether the resolution survived. Measure how many attempts you made and what each one told you. An attempt that breaks in week five and leaves you with a written note saying *where* and *why* is worth more than one that limps along to March on vague good intentions and fades without a lesson.

Concretely: when it breaks, and it will, write down the date, the place, who you were with, what you'd been doing in the hour before. Don't editorialise. Don't write "I was weak." Write "Saturday, wedding, third drink, outside with the smokers." That's a finding. Then plan the next attempt around that finding specifically, and start it as soon as you've written the note. Not next January. Now.

One attempt per year is a terrible experimental design. Four attempts in eighteen months, each one patching the hole the last one found, is how things actually get quit.

You're not failing. You're running trials. Just make sure you keep the results.

* **Security & Data Privacy:** AI doesn't know our threat model. It will happily suggest insecure cryptographic hashes or expose sensitive data loops if not caught.
* **Architectural Decisions:** AI solves for the immediate prompt, not for the system's long-term scalability or maintainability.
* **The "Hallucination" Tax:** Creating phantom libraries or methods that look perfectly logical but don't actually exist.
* **The Takeaway:** Never blindly commit code you don't understand well enough to explain to a peer. You own the code, not the assistant.

* **The Golden Rule:** The engineer whose name is on the pull request is 100% responsible for the code, regardless of who (or what) typed it.
